findings.message: The REPO_ROOT fallback `$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/..` is broken after the script moved from `scripts/ao-update.sh` (one level below repo root) to `packages/cli/src/assets/scripts/ao-update.sh`. One level up now resolves to `packages/cli/src/assets` (or `dist/assets` in the compiled package), not the repo root. Any direct invocation of the script without `AO_REPO_ROOT` set will `cd "$REPO_ROOT"` into the wrong directory, causing all git operations (fetch, pull, branch checks) to silently operate on the wrong path or fail. `runRepoScript` always passes `AO_REPO_ROOT`, so the `ao update` CLI path is safe, but direct shell invocation is broken.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: line 43 of ao-update.sh uses `$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/..'` as fallback for REPO_ROOT. After moving the script from `scripts/` (one level below repo root) to `packages/cli/src/assets/scripts/`, `..` resolves to `packages/cli/src/assets` in source checkouts and `dist/assets` in compiled packages — neither is the repo/package root. The CLI path via runRepoScript/executeScriptCommand always injects AO_REPO_ROOT so it is unaffected, but direct shell invocation without AO_REPO_ROOT silently uses the wrong directory.
findings.severity_justification: The CLI invocation path (primary usage) is safe because runRepoScript always injects AO_REPO_ROOT. Only direct shell invocation without the env var is broken, which is a secondary usage path.
findings.category_justification: The REPO_ROOT fallback computation resolves to the wrong directory after the script was relocated.

findings.message: Same broken REPO_ROOT fallback as ao-update.sh: `$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]")/..` now resolves to `dist/assets` instead of the package root. This cascades into the SCRIPT_LAYOUT auto-detection at lines 34-38, which checks `$REPO_ROOT/package.json` and `$REPO_ROOT/dist/index.js` to identify package installs. With the wrong REPO_ROOT, neither file exists, so `SCRIPT_LAYOUT` defaults to `source-checkout` on a direct package-install invocation. The doctor then runs source-checkout checks (looking for `node_modules`, `packages/core/dist`, etc.) against the wrong root, producing spurious FAIL results on a healthy package install.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: ao-doctor.sh line 31 has the same broken fallback as ao-update.sh. With REPO_ROOT incorrectly set to `dist/assets`, the SCRIPT_LAYOUT detection at lines 34-38 checks for `dist/assets/package.json` and `dist/assets/dist/index.js` — both nonexistent — so SCRIPT_LAYOUT defaults to `source-checkout`. This triggers source-checkout checks against the wrong root, producing spurious FAILs for node_modules, built packages, and the launcher entrypoint on an otherwise healthy package install.
findings.severity_justification: More impactful than the ao-update.sh case because the incorrect SCRIPT_LAYOUT detection causes a cascade of false FAILs in ao doctor, misleading users about the health of a valid package install. The CLI invocation path is safe since runRepoScript injects both AO_REPO_ROOT and AO_SCRIPT_LAYOUT.
findings.category_justification: The REPO_ROOT fallback resolves to the wrong directory, causing a chain of incorrect SCRIPT_LAYOUT detection and false-negative health checks in ao doctor.

findings.message: `handleGitUpdate` hardcodes `"npm-global"` as the fallback when `hasRepoScript("ao-update.sh")` returns false. `getUpdateCommand("npm-global")` returns `npm install -g @aoagents/ao@latest`, which silently converts a git source-checkout user to a global npm package install rather than directing them to rebuild with `pnpm --filter @aoagents/ao-cli build`. The correct fix would be an error message with a rebuild hint, not a method-switching npm install command.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: when hasRepoScript('ao-update.sh') returns false in handleGitUpdate (line 81-87), the code calls handleNpmUpdate(opts, 'npm-global'), which uses getUpdateCommand('npm-global') = 'npm install -g @aoagents/ao@latest'. This silently converts a git source-checkout install to a global npm install. The test at update.test.ts line 190-208 explicitly confirms this behavior. The finding correctly identifies that the appropriate response for a git install with missing scripts would be a rebuild hint rather than switching install methods.
findings.severity_justification: Running npm install -g on a git checkout user converts their install method without clearly warning them. This is a semantically wrong action — the user loses the ability to use source-checkout workflows (git pull, pnpm build). It only triggers when the update script is missing from the build output, an edge case, but the consequence is significant.
findings.category_justification: The fallback logic uses the wrong update command for the detected install method, resulting in incorrect behavior (method-switching npm install instead of a rebuild hint).

findings.message: `resolveScriptLayoutFromPath` returns `"package-install"` for any path containing `node_modules` (including local project installs and npx cache), while `classifyInstallPath` in `update-check.ts` returns `"unknown"` for local node_modules. This means a local/npx invocation sets `AO_SCRIPT_LAYOUT=package-install` on spawned shell scripts (causing doctor to run package-install checks) but `detectInstallMethod()` returns `"unknown"` (triggering `handleUnknownUpdate` in the update path). The two functions use different semantics for the same path type with no coordination.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: resolveScriptLayoutFromPath returns 'package-install' for any node_modules path (line 12-15), while classifyInstallPath returns 'unknown' for local/non-global node_modules. Both functions use their module's import.meta.url at runtime. For a local/npx install: doctor scripts get AO_SCRIPT_LAYOUT=package-install (correct), but detectInstallMethod() returns 'unknown' triggering handleUnknownUpdate (no script run). The two systems use divergent classification semantics for the same path type.
findings.severity_justification: The practical impact is limited — for local/npx installs, package-install doctor checks are actually appropriate, and the update 'unknown' path correctly prints a suggested command without doing anything destructive. The inconsistency is a maintainability and semantic clarity issue rather than a user-facing bug for most install types.
findings.category_justification: Two parallel classification systems in the same package with divergent semantics for the same path type, with no coordination or shared logic, creating a drift risk.

findings.message: `run_smoke_tests` references `$REPO_ROOT/packages/agent-orchestrator/bin/ao.js`, but that directory no longer exists — the wrapper package is at `packages/ao/bin/ao.js`. The smoke tests will always fail with a missing file error even on a healthy source checkout. This was present before the rename but the PR had the opportunity to fix it while touching this file, and the broken path now receives wider exposure since the script is bundled and more likely to be audited.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: ao-update.sh lines 61-63 reference $REPO_ROOT/packages/agent-orchestrator/bin/ao.js but packages/agent-orchestrator does not exist (renamed to packages/ao). The PR moved the script but didn't fix the path — the git log confirms c2358798 just did a rename without changing the stale reference. The tests mask this by creating a fake packages/agent-orchestrator directory. On a real source checkout, ao update smoke tests always fail.
findings.severity_justification: Smoke tests run by default on every ao update (only skipped with --skip-smoke). This means ao update always fails at the smoke test stage on any source checkout, even after a successful git pull and rebuild. The core update workflow is broken for all git-install users.
findings.category_justification: A hardcoded path references a directory that no longer exists, causing runtime failure in the primary update workflow.

findings.message: The `runRepoScript` function sets `cwd: process.cwd()`, which could cause scripts to fail if they are not run from the repository root. Scripts often make assumptions about the current working directory to find other files. The `doctor` and `update` commands are now more likely to be run from arbitrary directories, especially in a global install. Changing `cwd` to `repoRoot` would make script execution more predictable.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The cwd: process.cwd() is intentional. ao-update.sh explicitly does 'cd "$REPO_ROOT"' at line 90, so it doesn't rely on the spawn cwd. ao-doctor.sh's find_config() walks up from $PWD (line 83) to locate agent-orchestrator.yaml in the user's project directory — this requires process.cwd(), not repoRoot. The suggested fix would break config discovery. Additionally, the git history shows this was changed from repoRoot to process.cwd() in commit 76652c7c, confirming the choice is deliberate.
findings.severity_justification: The suggested fix would actually degrade the doctor command by breaking user-directory config discovery, making this a FP with potential harm if acted upon.
findings.category_justification: The finding makes an incorrect claim about script behavior — the cwd is intentionally process.cwd() to support config file discovery walking up from the user's working directory.

findings.message: The error message in `resolveScriptPath` does not check or handle the possibility of dynamically resolved script paths resulting in undefined behavior or runtime issues in non-standard environments.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding is generic and non-specific. resolveScriptPath constructs a deterministic path via resolve(CLI_DIST_ROOT, 'assets', 'scripts', scriptName), checks existence with existsSync, and throws a descriptive error if missing. There is no dynamic resolution ambiguity or undefined behavior. The finding does not identify a concrete scenario, input, or code path that causes a problem — 'non-standard environments' is unspecified boilerplate that could apply to any path resolution function.
findings.severity_justification: No concrete issue is identified; the claim is unverifiable and generic.
findings.category_justification: The finding loosely relates to error handling and environment-specific behavior, but identifies no actual reliability gap.

findings.message: `fetchLatestVersion` directly references the npm registry without retry logic or support for fallback mirrors, which can lead to failed updates in regions with npm registry connectivity issues.
findings.tp_fp_justification: fetchLatestVersion already handles failures gracefully — it catches all exceptions and returns null, has a 3-second AbortSignal timeout, and callers treat null as 'no update info available' without crashing. The suggestion for retry logic and fallback mirrors is a generic best-practice recommendation that could be copy-pasted to any fetch call in any codebase; it does not identify a specific bug or regression introduced by this PR. The code is also pre-existing and not modified by this PR.
findings.severity_justification: Version check failures degrade gracefully to 'no update info', so there is no user-visible breakage from a single failed fetch.
findings.category_justification: The finding loosely concerns network resilience, though it identifies no concrete failure scenario beyond generic connectivity concerns.

findings.message: `writeCache` relies on synchronous file system operations and does not handle failures robustly, potentially causing issues in environments with IO constraints or temporary locks on the cache directory.
findings.tp_fp_justification: writeCache already wraps all filesystem operations in try/catch with the explicit comment 'Best-effort — don't crash if cache dir is unwritable'. Any IO failure is silently caught and ignored, which is the correct behavior for an optional update-check cache. The finding incorrectly asserts the function does not handle failures robustly. The code is also pre-existing and not modified by this PR.
findings.severity_justification: No actual issue exists — failures are already handled gracefully.
findings.category_justification: The finding concerns filesystem error handling, though the claim is factually incorrect about the existing implementation.

findings.message: The `createHealthyPackageInstall` test helper writes to a nested 'dist/assets/scripts' path without validating the intermediate layer structure integrity, leading to potential test fragility in CI/CD.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The function uses mkdirSync with { recursive: true }, which creates all intermediate directories atomically. There is no mechanism by which the nested path creation could partially fail while leaving the function in an inconsistent state. The finding does not identify any concrete failure scenario or CI/CD condition that would cause the test to break — it is a vague, unverifiable claim about 'structure integrity' that does not apply to this code pattern.
findings.severity_justification: No actual fragility identified; the code uses the standard Node.js recursive mkdir pattern correctly.
findings.category_justification: The finding concerns test helper implementation quality.

findings.message: In `registerUpdate`, the `process.exit` calls make it harder to mock or integrate this command within programmatic interfaces like automated scripts or other CLI compositions.
findings.tp_fp_justification: process.exit is standard and expected in CLI command handlers — it is the correct way to signal exit codes in a Commander-based CLI. The pattern is used throughout the codebase (update.ts, doctor.ts, etc.) and the test suite already mocks it with exitOverride(). The finding is a generic best-practice observation about testability that could be copy-pasted to any CLI command file without modification; it identifies no concrete bug or regression introduced by this PR.
findings.severity_justification: No actual issue — process.exit is appropriate in CLI entry points and is already handled in tests via Commander's exitOverride.
findings.category_justification: The finding loosely concerns code design and testability, but identifies no specific actionable problem in this codebase.

findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified by checking all three commits in the PR branch. Before the PR: checked scripts/ao-update.sh && .git (AO-specific). At c2358798 (part of this PR): weakened to just .git. At HEAD (76652c7c): still just .git. The isAgentOrchestratorRepoRoot approach shown in the PR diff was never committed. The weakened check means any non-AO path 4 levels below a .git dir gets classified as 'git', potentially triggering destructive update operations in the wrong repo.
findings.severity_justification: A false 'git' classification causes ao update to run git pull, pnpm install, pnpm build, and npm link against an unrelated enclosing git repo — potentially destructive operations on the wrong codebase. The scenario requires a non-node_modules vendored copy of the CLI, making it an edge case, but the impact when triggered is significant.
findings.category_justification: The weakened install detection logic produces incorrect classifications for edge-case path structures, leading to wrong update behavior.

findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: resolveRepoRoot() at line 30-32 accepts AO_REPO_ROOT without validation and propagates it to shell scripts that run git pull, pnpm install, pnpm build, and npm link against $REPO_ROOT. The PR diff showed isValidRepoRootForLayout validation being added, but it was never committed — the actual HEAD code is bare resolve(override). The finding correctly identifies missing validation that was planned but omitted.
findings.severity_justification: Exploitation requires an attacker to already control the user's process environment, at which point there are more direct attack paths. The realistic risk is misconfiguration rather than an active attack. The operations triggered (git pull, pnpm build, npm link) are destructive but only to the user's own filesystem.
findings.category_justification: An environment variable accepted without validation is propagated to shell scripts performing filesystem and git mutations, which is an ambient-privilege elevation path.

findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: resolveScriptLayout() at line 34-40 accepts AO_SCRIPT_LAYOUT unconditionally. An ambient or user-set AO_SCRIPT_LAYOUT overrides the auto-detected layout, causing ao doctor to skip checks appropriate to the actual install type. The PR diff showed an AO_DEV=1 guard being added, but it was not committed at SHA 76652c7c. The env var has no legitimate user-facing purpose beyond TS-to-shell context passing, making the unconditional acceptance an oversight.
findings.severity_justification: The impact is limited to ao doctor producing misleading results (wrong checks for the actual install type). There's no data loss or direct exploit path — a user would need to intentionally or accidentally set AO_SCRIPT_LAYOUT in their environment. The affected tool is diagnostic, not transactional.
findings.category_justification: An internal communication env var is exposed as an unguarded override, causing diagnostic checks to run against the wrong install-type assumptions.

findings.tp_fp_justification: The TOCTOU is real: hasRepoScript (existsSync at T1) and resolveScriptPath (existsSync at T2) check the same file twice with no atomic guarantee. If the file vanishes between checks, resolveScriptPath throws and the npm fallback is bypassed — executeScriptCommand catches the error and prints the raw message before process.exit(1). The 'raw thrown error' framing is slightly inaccurate since executeScriptCommand does catch it, but the friendly handleNpmUpdate fallback is indeed bypassed. The suggested single-check approach is architecturally cleaner.
findings.severity_justification: The TOCTOU window is microseconds (no async operation between the two existsSync calls), making accidental triggering extremely unlikely. When triggered, the user sees an error message and clean exit rather than the npm fallback — inconvenient but not dangerous.
findings.category_justification: The two-check pattern creates a theoretical race between file existence check and use, and bypasses the intended graceful fallback path.

findings.message: **Nit / UX consistency (re: the catch at L427):** `update.ts` (L87-99) catches `Script not found: ao-update.sh` and prints the actionable *"rebuild with `pnpm --filter @aoagents/ao-cli build`"* hint. The equivalent catch here just prints the raw `resolveScriptPath` error. Worth adding a parallel branch so a broken packaged install surfaces the same fix instruction when `ao doctor` is the first command the user tries? Low stakes, but `doctor` is exactly where users land when something is wrong.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding's premise is factually incorrect for SHA 76652c7c. update.ts lines 87-99 do not contain a 'Script not found' catch with a rebuild hint — that code appeared in the PR diff's intermediate version but was superseded by the hasRepoScript pre-check + executeScriptCommand pattern in the final commit. Both doctor.ts and update.ts handle missing scripts through the same raw-error path (executeScriptCommand/runRepoScript catches and prints err.message). The UX inconsistency the finding describes does not exist at this SHA.
findings.severity_justification: The finding is incorrect about the comparison, making it FP. The underlying suggestion to improve doctor.ts error messaging has merit but is a minor UX nit.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about user-facing error messages and actionable hints, which is a UX/documentation concern.

findings.message: **Question:** `isValidRepoRootForLayout` (above, L54) is called with `DEFAULT_SCRIPT_LAYOUT` — frozen at module load — but `resolveScriptLayout()` below honors `AO_SCRIPT_LAYOUT` when `AO_DEV=1`. So the dev combo `AO_DEV=1 AO_SCRIPT_LAYOUT=package-install AO_REPO_ROOT=/path/to/installed/cli` running from a source checkout has its layout override accepted but its repo-root override rejected (validator still demands a source-checkout repo). Intentional guard, or should the validator also consult `resolveScriptLayout()`? A comment pinning down which override wins when they disagree would help future-me.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding references isValidRepoRootForLayout (L54) and the AO_DEV=1 gate in resolveScriptLayout(), but neither exists in the committed code at SHA 76652c7c. Both features appeared in the PR diff but were not committed — resolveRepoRoot() has no validation logic and resolveScriptLayout() has no AO_DEV gate. The described override conflict cannot occur because the code it depends on isn't present.
findings.severity_justification: The finding is FP; no actual code issue exists at this SHA.
findings.category_justification: The finding is a documentation/clarity question about interaction between two override mechanisms, which is a maintainability concern when those mechanisms exist.

findings.message: spotted a stale path rh. this has to be `$REPO_ROOT/packages/ao/bin/ao.js`
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: ao-doctor.sh lines 325 and 330 reference $REPO_ROOT/packages/agent-orchestrator/bin/ao.js in the source-checkout branch of check_runtime_sanity(). packages/agent-orchestrator does not exist — the package is at packages/ao with bin/ao.js present. This causes the source-checkout runtime sanity check to always FAIL on a healthy source checkout, even when everything is working correctly.
findings.severity_justification: ao doctor check_runtime_sanity always fails on a source checkout because the referenced path doesn't exist, producing a false FAIL result. Since ao doctor exits with code 1 when FAIL_COUNT > 0, ao doctor always reports an unhealthy environment for source checkout users even when everything is fine.
findings.category_justification: A hardcoded path references a directory that no longer exists, causing a runtime check to produce incorrect FAIL results.
